verdicts.quote: There is a parking lot that is located in the behind position of the store.
verdicts.reason: This is not natural English; use a normal behind phrase such as “There is a parking lot behind the store.”

verdicts.quote: later or slower than planned, or not as far along as other people
verdicts.reason: The definition wrongly limits comparative progress to people, although this use also applies to work, projects, and processes.
This is the adverb use of behind, not the preposition use in this entry.

verdicts.quote: giving support or encouragement to sb or sth
verdicts.reason: The definition uses prohibited abbreviations in prose.

verdicts.quote: giving support or encouragement to sb or sth
verdicts.reason: A preposition definition should state the relation, for example “in support of someone or something,” rather than use a participle phrase.

verdicts.quote: later or slower than planned, or not as far along as other people
verdicts.reason: The entry needs a separate prepositional sense for being late in payment, as in “behind on the rent” or “behind with payments.”
This adverb example conflicts with the entry’s preposition part of speech and its headword-and-part-of-speech scope.
The common prepositional use meaning late in paying or completing something is not covered.

verdicts.quote: behind someone in a race, game, score, or election
verdicts.reason: The common prepositional use meaning at a lower position or score than another competitor or side is not covered.
The example does not fit sense 2 because it uses adverbial behind meaning “in a place after leaving,” not prepositional behind meaning less advanced.

summary: The entry has generally sound basic spatial, support, and cause senses, but it contains one unnatural example, one out-of-part-of-speech example, prohibited abbreviations in a definition, and missing common prepositional uses for arrears and competitive position.
